tagline: Up Shell Canyon in switchbacks, down the gentle side to Dayton.
intro: About four miles out of Shell, a town named for the fossil shells found around it, US 14 reaches the national forest and starts up the Bighorns in a run of switchbacks and squeezes through Shell Canyon, where at times the creek is hidden far below the roadway. At Granite Pass, 9,033 feet, it tops out among windswept vegetation and solid granite. The way down the east side toward Dayton is steady and not as steep.
The names take some sorting out. Anything the federal government runs is Bighorn, one word, and everything else is Big Horn, two. All of it is named for the bighorn sheep.

moments.title: Shell Falls
moments.text: On the north side of the highway Shell Creek dives 120 feet down a slide of Precambrian granite into the gorge, with nature trails and signs at the stop.

moments.title: Granite Creek
moments.text: A sign at the picnic area points out the damaged trees across on the opposite mountain, where a freak tornado came through in 1959.

moments.title: Fallen City
moments.text: At the forest boundary, 6.5 miles west of Dayton, an overlook takes in the Powder River Basin and Fallen City, a field of limestone blocks that toppled onto the rocks below.

practical: WYDOT notes the two-lane byway can close for short periods in heavy winter or early-spring snow, while summer and fall travel is normally not interrupted.
